candidates.next_evidence: Verify MW under development, signed bookings/pre-leasing, power availability by metro, capex intensity, and whether lease spreads/returns are improving or being diluted by grid and construction costs.
candidates.node_relation: Direct asset owner and platform for hyperscale/enterprise data-center capacity; electricity availability, interconnection speed, and high-reliability power are core constraints for its growth.
candidates.theme_relation: AI workloads increase demand for high-density data-center campuses, shifting value toward operators that already control powered shells, interconnection relationships, and global colocation capacity.
candidates.why_include: Digital Realty is one of the clearest public-market mappings from AI compute demand into physical data-center capacity. Its March 2026 investor materials explicitly frame AI as affecting customer engagement, data-center design, and product offerings, and state that PlatformDIGITAL is positioned to benefit from AI training and inference demand.

candidates.next_evidence: Track xScale leasing, incremental MW delivery, power-utilization disclosures, customer concentration, and any evidence that power scarcity is either supporting pricing or delaying revenue recognition.
candidates.node_relation: Direct data-center platform with large global IBX and xScale capacity expansion; AI and cloud demand creates incremental power, cabinet, and interconnection needs.
candidates.sector_or_industry: Data center REIT / interconnection and colocation platform
candidates.theme_relation: Equinix maps the Energy theme into the demand node because AI/cloud customers need reliable powered capacity and low-latency interconnection before upstream grid assets can fully catch up.
candidates.why_include: Equinix disclosed 52 active major development projects across 35 metros as of January 2026, expected to deliver more than 55,000 retail cabinets and more than 100 MW of xScale capacity through 2028, tying the company directly to AI/cloud capacity expansion.

candidates.next_evidence: Check Virginia SCC filings, large-load tariff design, PJM DOM-zone load forecasts, interconnection deposits, capex recovery, and whether ratepayer-protection rules shift economics away from shareholders or data-center customers.
candidates.node_relation: Regulated utility serving Virginia, including Northern Virginia data-center load; exposed to transmission, distribution, and generation investment required to connect large loads.
candidates.theme_relation: Dominion is a utility-side expression of the AI/data-center load-growth node: the bottleneck is not AI chips themselves but the ability to interconnect and serve committed load at utility scale.
candidates.why_include: Dominion's 2025 annual-report filing states that much of its growth is being driven by the booming data-center industry and that it has been connecting an average of 15 data centers per year, while third-party reporting in 2026 cited a data-center pipeline above 48 GW in various stages of contracting.

candidates.next_evidence: Look for signed data-center PPAs, behind-the-meter deals, nuclear uprate/relicensing economics, ERCOT/PJM capacity-price sensitivity, and disclosure of large commercial customer demand.
candidates.node_relation: Dispatchable generation owner with nuclear/gas/retail power exposure; potential beneficiary if AI/data-center campuses require firm power and reliability faster than new transmission can be built.
candidates.sector_or_industry: Integrated power generation and retail electricity
candidates.theme_relation: Vistra maps to the supply response to the demand node: large data-center loads increase the value of firm, dispatchable power, especially in constrained markets where reliability and speed-to-power matter.
candidates.why_include: Vistra describes itself as a leading integrated retail electricity and power-generation company and, in 2026 CERAWeek materials, emphasized rapidly growing energy demand, rising data-center demand, reliability, and the role of nuclear energy. candidates.next_evidence: Validate data-center revenue mix, backlog quality, customer concentration, project-margin sustainability, labor availability, and whether growth depends on a small number of hyperscale projects.
candidates.node_relation: Second-order supplier to the node: designs and installs integrated electrical and technology systems for data centers and other commercial/industrial end markets.

memory_update.text: Add DLR and EQIX as direct data-center asset-owner/platform candidates for the AI/electrification load-growth node; they convert AI compute demand into powered-capacity demand.
Add Dominion Energy as a regulated-utility candidate because Virginia data-center growth creates direct load, grid-connection, and capex-recovery exposure.
Add Vistra as a firm-power/dispatchable-generation candidate, but retain inference status until signed data-center PPAs or large-load contracts are verified.
Add IES Holdings as a second-order electrical/technology infrastructure contractor with explicit data-center end-market exposure.

Future passes should separately map transformer/switchgear suppliers, backup-generation vendors, utility-scale gas turbine suppliers, grid software/forecasting vendors, and regional utilities in ERCOT/PJM/MISO/SERC with large-load tariff filings.

node: AI/data-center and broad electrification load growth
summary: Expanded the universe for the demand-side node by adding five US-listed companies with direct exposure to AI/data-center load growth or the power/interconnection bottleneck around that load. The additions emphasize data-center asset owners with secured capacity, a Virginia utility exposed to the largest US data-center cluster, a dispatchable power generator likely exposed to large-load procurement, and an electrical/technology contractor with explicit data-center end-market exposure. This is research support only, not a buy/sell recommendation.
